title: Who gets to speak at the World Court? Parties, counsel and the missing ethics code
subtitle: Only states can be parties. They can bring almost anyone as counsel. And the Court itself has no code of conduct for those counsel, so who can discipline an advocate depends on which country’s bar they belong to, if any.
summary: Before the International Court of Justice, only states may be parties in contentious cases. Each state is represented by an agent and may bring counsel and advocates of its choosing; the Statute sets no qualification for them. The Court’s Practice Directions deal with conflicts of position, such as former judges appearing as counsel, but not with honesty, and counsel “are not subject under international law to any compulsory code of conduct”. English barristers carry their own rules with them wherever they appear; academics who are not admitted anywhere may carry none. The Genocide Convention case South Africa v. Israel shows the system at work: members of one London chambers on opposite sides, and more than a dozen states intervening.
scope: International Court of Justice · Who may be a party, who may represent a party, which conduct rules bind them, who could enforce those rules, and how third states and NGOs take part. English professional rules are covered as one example of home-bar rules. Covers documents checked up to 5 November 2026.
status_note: The Statute, the Rules of Court, Practice Directions, General Assembly resolution 90(I), ICJ press releases, the ICTY code and Bar Council guidance were read from their official texts on 5 November 2026, with the Rules of Court checked again on 12 November 2026. Some academic sources and the January 2024 verbatim record could not be retrieved; claims resting on them were removed or are labelled. Chapters marked “Our analysis” are our views. This is legal research and public education, not legal advice.

sections.title: 1. The door: who can be a party?
sections.intro: The Court decides disputes between states and gives advisory opinions. Each has its own door.

paragraphs.text: “Only states may be parties in cases before the Court.” Individuals, companies and NGOs cannot bring or defend a contentious case.
Advisory proceedings work differently: states and intergovernmental organisations may present statements under Article 66 of the Statute. NGOs have a narrower side route, described in chapter 7.

sections.title: 2. The team: agents, counsel and advocates
sections.intro: Who stands up for a state, and who chooses them. The Court requires an agent and regulates that role. It does not decide who a state may appoint, or how the appointment is made at home.

paragraphs.text: “The parties shall be represented by agents. They may have the assistance of counsel or advocates before the Court.” The agent is the state’s formal representative. The Statute says nothing about who counsel and advocates must be: no admission, no qualification, no nationality rule. In practice states choose national lawyers, foreign barristers, professors and diplomats.
Example: Vaughan Lowe KC, a member of Essex Court Chambers in London, lists South Africa v. Israel among his reported cases as counsel, “ICJ 2024- (for South Africa)”.

entries.title: The Court regulates the agent’s role, not who a state appoints

paragraphs.text: The Rules of Court fill in how that agency works, once a case has begun. Article 40 says that, except in the special case of an application awaiting the other state’s consent to jurisdiction, “all steps on behalf of the parties after proceedings have been instituted shall be taken by agents.” Agents must have an address for service at the seat of the Court; communications to the agents “shall be considered as having been addressed to the parties themselves.” The applicant (or the party notifying a special agreement) must state the name of its agent, and the other party must inform the Court of the name of its agent. Article 60, paragraph 2, adds a further formal act: at the end of a party’s last statement at the hearing, “its agent, without recapitulation of the arguments, shall read that party’s final submissions.” Article 58, paragraph 2, lets the Court, after hearing the parties, settle “the number of counsel and advocates to be heard on behalf of each party.” These are rules about the role of the agent, and about how the hearing is run.

Neither the Statute nor the Rules of Court set any qualification, admission, nationality or method of appointment for the agent, or for counsel or advocates. The Court must be told the name of the agent; it does not choose the person, and it does not regulate how a state makes that choice. Who is appointed, and by what domestic process, is left to each state under its own arrangements. Practice Directions VII and VIII, discussed below, limit certain conflicts of position. They still do not tell a state whom it may appoint in the ordinary case, or how to do so at home.

sources.locator: Article 42: the duty to have agents, with no eligibility rule
Article 40: the name of the agent is notified, not selected, by the Court

sections.title: 3. The vacuum: no ICJ ethics code
sections.intro: The striking fact about the world’s highest court.

paragraphs.text: Two practitioners writing in the American Society of International Law’s proceedings put it plainly: individuals appearing before the Court “are not subject under international law to any compulsory code of conduct”.
The Court’s Practice Directions do contain rules about counsel, but they deal with conflicts of position, such as a former judge appearing as counsel. None addresses honesty or misleading the Court.

entries.title: The nearest substitute: the Hague Principles

paragraphs.text: In 2010 a study group of the International Law Association presented the Hague Principles on Ethical Standards for Counsel Appearing before International Courts and Tribunals. They are soft law: guidance that binds no one unless a court adopts it.

entries.title: Other tribunals chose a binding code

paragraphs.text: The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia adopted a code of conduct for counsel with its own disciplinary panel. Article 4: “If there is any inconsistency between this Code and any other codes of practice and ethics governing counsel, the terms of this Code prevail in respect of counsel’s conduct before the Tribunal.”

sections.title: 4. The patchwork: one team, several codes
sections.intro: Because the Court has no code, each lawyer brings their own, or none.

entries.title: Different rules for the same conduct

paragraphs.text: National conduct rules “can vary considerably across different jurisdictions”, and “Counsel who are academics or are not admitted in any jurisdiction may not be subject to any conduct rules.”

entries.title: English barristers carry their rules with them

table.caption: Who on a state’s team is bound by what
rows: BSB Handbook wherever they appear, plus applicable foreign rules unless inconsistent with the Core Duties
That country’s rules, to the extent they apply abroad
Their state’s employment rules; no bar code
The non-binding Hague Principles, if they choose to follow them

paragraphs.text: Bar Council guidance: the BSB Handbook “applies to your conduct in court and before tribunals … wherever those courts and tribunals may be sitting”. Sections 2.B, 2.C and 2.D apply “whether you are practising or providing legal services in England and Wales or elsewhere”. Rule rC13 adds a duty to comply with applicable foreign conduct rules, unless they are inconsistent with the Core Duties.
Foreign work is not subject to the cab-rank rule, so an English barrister may decline it without breaching the duty to accept work in their field (rC30.5).

sections.title: 5. Enforcement: who can do anything?
sections.intro: If no one has a code, who holds an advocate to account?

entries.title: The Court and the home regulator

paragraphs.text: The Court controls its own procedure and weighs the evidence and arguments put to it. We found no published disciplinary procedure for counsel before the ICJ. A home regulator can, in principle, act on conduct abroad where its rules apply; for English barristers, the BSB. We found no published instance of a regulator disciplining counsel for conduct before the ICJ. That is a gap in our search, not proof that none exists.

Agents, counsel and advocates “shall enjoy the privileges and immunities necessary to the independent exercise of their duties.” General Assembly resolution 90(I) of 1946 gives effect to this during their missions, and says the immunities exist in the interests of justice, not for personal benefit; for counsel representing a state, the state may waive them.

Our analysis: these protections aim at legal process interfering with the work. Whether they would limit a home regulator’s discipline is, as far as we found, unsettled. Domestic offences such as perverting the course of justice protect a country’s own justice system; in our assessment they are unlikely to reach conduct in The Hague, but we found no authority either way.

sections.title: 6. Procedural rules that do exist
sections.intro: The Court regulates conflicts of position, not honesty.

paragraphs.text: Direction VII: parties should not nominate as judge ad hoc anyone acting, or who acted in the previous three years, as agent, counsel or advocate in another case, nor appoint as counsel anyone sitting as judge ad hoc elsewhere. Direction VIII: parties should not designate as agent, counsel or advocate anyone who in the previous three years was a Member of the Court, a judge ad hoc, Registrar, Deputy-Registrar or a senior Registry official.
Nothing in the Directions corresponds to the English rule against knowingly or recklessly misleading the court.

sections.title: 7. Third voices: interventions and NGOs
sections.intro: States can join a case; NGOs can only leave a document in the building.

paragraphs.text: Article 62: a state with “an interest of a legal nature which may be affected by the decision” may ask to intervene. Article 63: when a convention is being interpreted, every state party to it “has the right to intervene”, but “the construction given by the judgment will be equally binding upon it.”

entries.title: South Africa v. Israel draws a crowd
entries.kind: Court press releases and news reporting

table.caption: Interventions confirmed in the sources we checked

paragraphs.text: By 2 October 2024 the Court listed Nicaragua (Article 62, January 2024), Palestine (Articles 62 and 63) and Article 63 declarations from Colombia, Libya, Mexico, Spain, Türkiye, Chile and the Maldives. On 11 March 2026 the Netherlands and Iceland filed declarations, as reported citing the Court. On 12 March 2026 Namibia, the United States, Hungary and Fiji filed Article 63 declarations. That is at least 15 states; others filed in between, and we have not reconciled a full count.

entries.title: NGOs: a side door, advisory cases only

paragraphs.text: Under Practice Direction XII an international NGO may submit a written statement on its own initiative in advisory proceedings. It “is not to be considered part of the case file”, is “placed in a designated location in the Peace Palace”, and participating states and organisations are told where to find it. There is no equivalent route in contentious cases such as South Africa v. Israel.

sections.title: 8. Case study: same chambers, opposite sides
sections.intro: Our companion page on this is in preparation and not yet published.

paragraphs.text: Vaughan Lowe KC’s Essex Court Chambers profile lists South Africa v. Israel, “ICJ 2024- (for South Africa)”. Malcolm Shaw KC’s profile at the same chambers lists “Government of Israel (lead counsel) in case before the International Court of Justice, (2023 -)”. The chambers describes itself as “not a firm or a partnership but rather an unincorporated association of self-employed sole practitioners”.

Our analysis: under English rules that arrangement is permitted. Before the ICJ it sits inside the patchwork above: home-bar rules for the English barristers, other rules or none for their colleagues on each team. Shared membership tells us nothing, on its own, about any private discussion, and we allege none.

sections.title: 9. How can anyone else be there?
sections.intro: A private person cannot appoint themselves to a case.

table.caption: Routes into a case
rows: A place on a legal team as counsel, adviser or assistant
An advisory-case statement kept at the Peace Palace, outside the case file
Watching or reporting public hearings, under the Court’s current arrangements

paragraphs.text: States choose their teams freely, interventions are for states only, and NGOs have Practice Direction XII in advisory cases. Public hearings can be watched; check the Court’s current arrangements for the public gallery and media accreditation, which we have not set out here.

sections.title: Questions
sections.intro: Our questions, for readers and for the Court.

paragraphs.text: 1. Should the ICJ adopt a binding counsel code, as the Yugoslavia tribunal did? 2. If so, who would enforce it: the Court, the state, or home bars? 3. Should states disclose which conduct rules bind each member of their team? 4. Is it fair that an English barrister and an unregulated academic on the same team face different exposure for identical conduct?

The Statute, Rules of Court, Practice Directions, resolution 90(I), ICJ press releases, the ICTY code, Bar Council guidance and the chambers profiles were read on 5 November 2026, with the Rules of Court (Articles 40, 58 and 60) checked again on 12 November 2026 when the section on what the Court does and does not regulate in appointments was added. The draft supplied to us was checked line by line; claims we could not trace to a document we read were removed or labelled.

We could not retrieve the January 2024 verbatim record (CR 2024/2), so delegation lists are not quoted here. Academic works by Skinner, Sarvarian and Longobardo, and a Leiden-hosted ASIL article that the draft mislabelled, were not read and are not relied on. The total number of intervening states is not reconciled. We found no published case of a regulator disciplining counsel for ICJ conduct; that is a search result, not a finding.
